## Descripción

La crema dermatológica CUTAMYCON te ayuda a apoyar el tratamiento de afecciones de la piel en mascotas con un enfoque antibacteriano y antimicótico. Su fórmula combina ingredientes activos para actuar sobre la piel con control de hongos y bacterias, además de contribuir a calmar la irritación.

Material y construcción verificados: crema dermatológica veterinaria con gentamicina, clotrimazol, betametasona y óxido de zinc.

 

##### Características

  * Brinda acción antibacteriana para apoyar el control de bacterias sensibles.
  * Ofrece acción antimicótica para ayudar a controlar hongos en la piel.
  * Contribuye a disminuir la inflamación y la irritación cutánea.
  * Apoya el alivio de reacciones asociadas a la piel sensible.
  * Favorece la recuperación de la piel con efecto cicatrizante.
  * Su textura en crema facilita una aplicación tópica localizada y precisa.
  * Ayuda a mejorar la tolerancia de la piel al no irritar y no manchar.

 

##### Aplicaciones Recomendadas

  * Para apoyar el tratamiento de dermatitis con componente micótico.
  * Para lesiones de la piel asociadas a bacterias sensibles.
  * Para zonas con enrojecimiento, picazón o irritación cutánea.
  * Para el manejo tópico de afecciones dermatológicas en mascotas.
  * Para aplicaciones donde se requiere una crema de acción múltiple en la piel.

 

##### Especificaciones Técnicas

  * Presentación: crema de 35 g.
  * Principios activos: gentamicina, clotrimazol, betametasona y óxido de zinc.
  * Acción terapéutica: antibacteriana, antimicótica, antiinflamatoria, antialérgica y cicatrizante.
  * Uso: dermatológico veterinario.

Title: CREMA: Collinear Resonance for Exotic Molecules and Atoms
Authors: Fabian C. Pastrana Cruz, Shane G. Wilkins, Alex J. Brinson, Paul Fischer, Mathieu Flayol, Derick Gonzalez-Acevedo, Jackson Hacias, Jason Huskey, Haruka Kakioka, Carina Kanitz, Jonas Karthein, Simon Lechner, Stephan Malbrunot-Ettenauer, Scott Moroch, Jose M. Munoz, Moritz P. Reiter, Mikael Reponen, Lutz Schweikhard, Silviu M. Udrescu, Adam R. Vernon, Markus Vilen, Ronald F. Garcia Ruiz
Date: Wed Oct 21 23:08:18 2026

The Collinear Resonance for Exotic Molecules and Atoms (CREMA) setup has been developed and commissioned at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology's Laboratory for Nuclear Science. The instrument combines the Doppler-suppressed resolution of the collinear fast-beam geometry with the selectivity of resonance ionization, for precision measurements of hyperfine structure and isotope shifts in atoms and molecules. We describe the setup, including the ion-optical simulations in which a multi-objective evolutionary algorithm provided the starting settings for the beam transport, and report commissioning measurements of the hyperfine structure of 133Cs. The extracted hyperfine constants agree with literature values within one standard deviation, demonstrating the operational readiness of the setup. CREMA mirrors the Resonance Ionization Spectroscopy Experiment at the Facility for Rare Isotope Beams and serves as its offline counterpart for the development of laser ionization schemes and techniques for future studies of exotic atoms and molecules.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
CutMix: Regularization Strategy to Train Strong Classifiers with Localizable Features (https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.04899)
citeturn233academia7 [wordlim: 200] Published: 7.5 years ago; 
Title: CutMix: Regularization Strategy to Train Strong Classifiers with Localizable Features
Authors: Sangdoo Yun, Dongyoon Han, Seong Joon Oh, Sanghyuk Chun, Junsuk Choe, Youngjoon Yoo
Date: Mon May 13 08:10:22 2019

Regional dropout strategies have been proposed to enhance the performance of convolutional neural network classifiers. They have proved to be effective for guiding the model to attend on less discriminative parts of objects (e.g. leg as opposed to head of a person), thereby letting the network generalize better and have better object localization capabilities. On the other hand, current methods for regional dropout remove informative pixels on training images by overlaying a patch of either black pixels or random noise. Such removal is not desirable because it leads to information loss and inefficiency during training. We therefore propose the CutMix augmentation strategy: patches are cut and pasted among training images where the ground truth labels are also mixed proportionally to the area of the patches. By making efficient use of training pixels and retaining the regularization effect of regional dropout, CutMix consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art augmentation strategies on CIFAR and ImageNet classification tasks, as well as on the ImageNet weakly-supervised localization task. Moreover, unlike previous augmentation methods, our CutMix-trained ImageNet classifier, when used as a pretrained model, results in consistent performance gains in Pascal detection and MS-COCO image captioning benchmarks. We also show that CutMix improves the model robustness against input corruptions and its out-of-distribution detection performances. Source code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/clovaai/CutMix-PyTorch .--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREMA: Generalizable and Efficient Video-Language Reasoning via Multimodal Modular Fusion (https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.05889)
citeturn233academia8 [wordlim: 200] Published: 2.7 years ago; 
Title: CREMA: Generalizable and Efficient Video-Language Reasoning via Multimodal Modular Fusion
Authors: Shoubin Yu, Jaehong Yoon, Mohit Bansal
Date: Thu Feb  8 18:27:22 2024

Despite impressive advancements in recent multimodal reasoning approaches, they are still limited in flexibility and efficiency, as these models typically process only a few fixed modality inputs and require updates to numerous parameters. This paper tackles these critical challenges and proposes CREMA, a generalizable, highly efficient, and modular modality-fusion framework that can incorporate any new modality to enhance video reasoning. We first augment multiple informative modalities (such as optical flow, 3D point cloud, audio, thermal heatmap, and touch map) from given videos without extra human annotation by leveraging sensors or existing pre-trained models. Next, we introduce a query transformer with multiple parameter-efficient modules associated with each accessible modality. It projects diverse modality features to the LLM token embedding space, allowing the model to integrate different data types for response generation. Furthermore, we propose a novel progressive multimodal fusion design supported by a lightweight fusion module and modality-sequential training strategy. It helps compress information across various assisting modalities, maintaining computational efficiency in the LLM while improving performance. We validate our method on 7 video-language reasoning tasks assisted by diverse modalities, including conventional VideoQA and Video-Audio/3D/Touch/Thermal QA, and achieve better/equivalent performance against strong multimodal LLMs, including OneLLM, BLIP-2, and SeViLA while reducing over 90% trainable parameters. We provide extensive analyses of CREMA, including the impact of each modality on reasoning domains, the design of the fusion module, and example visualizations.
